candidates.context: This guidance is intended to address questions that have been raised about the provisions of the 16 Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) that relate to generic drug exclusivity, which 17 commonly is known as 180-day exclusivity for generic drug products. As a general matter, the 18 Food and Drug Administration (FDA or the Agency) has implemented these statutory provisions 19 within the context of application-specific decisions. Some FDA decisions have been made 20 publicly available (e.g., in FDA citizen petition responses and documents released in litigation). 21 In addition, in certain circumstances where a novel issue of interpretation was raised by a 22 particular factual scenario regarding forfeiture of 180-day exclusivity, FDA has opened a public 23 docket or otherwise sought comment from affected parties in advance of taking an action. candidates.statement: The process for obtaining approval to market an innovator drug approved under a new drug 52 application (NDA) differs from that for obtaining approval to market a generic drug under an 53 ANDA. A sponsor of an innovator drug must submit an NDA, which must contain, among other 54 things, a demonstration of the safety and effectiveness of the drug for the conditions of use for 55 which approval is sought. 5 In its application, an NDA applicant must submit information for 56 each patent that claims the drug or method of using the drug and for which a claim of patent 57 infringement could reasonably be asserted against a person engaged in the unlicensed 58 manufacture, use, or sale of the drug product. 6 Upon approval of an NDA, FDA publishes this 59 patent information in its publication Approved Drug Products with Therapeutic Equivalence 60 Evaluations , known as the Orange Book. 7

Instead, the applicant 64 relies on FDA’s previous finding that the reference listed drug (RLD) 8 relied upon by the ANDA 65 applicant is safe and effective. The ANDA applicant must identify the RLD on which it seeks to 66 rely and, among other things, demonstrate, with limited exceptions, that the proposed generic 67 drug has the same active ingredient(s), route of administration, dosage form, and strength as the 68 RLD. 9 A generic drug also must have the same conditions of use and the same labeling as the 69 RLD (except for certain permissible labeling differences), 10 and the applicant must demonstrate 70 that its proposed generic drug is bioequivalent to the RLD. 11

candidates.context: C. 180-day Exclusivity and Patents 351 No. An applicant potentially may retain eligibility for 180-day exclusivity even if it is not sued 356 as a result of its qualifying paragraph IV certification or, if sued, the case is resolved, for 357 example, through settlement that allows the applicant to enter the market before the patent 358 expires. 39

candidates.statement: Yes. An NDA holder can request that FDA remove a patent from the Orange Book in certain 364 circumstances: for example, if a court declared the patent invalid. However, if an NDA holder 365 requests that a patent be removed from the Orange Book and one or more first applicants are 366 already eligible for 180-day exclusivity based on a paragraph IV certification to that patent, FDA 367 will not remove the patent until any 180-day exclusivity stemming from the listed patent has 368 expired, or has been extinguished or relinquished. 40 Until the patent is removed from the Orange 369 Book―after any associated 180-day exclusivity has expired or has been extinguished or 370 relinquished―ANDA applicants must submit or maintain appropriate certifications to the patent 371 notwithstanding the NDA holder’s request to remove the patent. This practice ensures that NDA 372 holders cannot unilaterally extinguish an ANDA applicant’s eligibility for 180-day exclusivity 373 by requesting removal of the patent from the Orange Book prior to ANDA approval. 41 In such 374 circumstances, FDA will indicate in the Orange Book that the NDA holder has requested 375 removal of the patent. 42

candidates.statement: This interpretation of the statute effectuates the goals of the Hatch-Waxman Amendments. The 392 180-day exclusivity provisions were drafted to give ANDA applicants an incentive to be the first 393 to challenge a listed patent, potentially removing that patent as a barrier to approval. Once a 394 listed patent expires and is no longer a barrier to ANDA approval, there is no longer a need to 395 provide an incentive to challenge it in court. Thus, an expired patent does not serve as the basis 396 for a 180-day exclusivity award, and 180-day exclusivity does not extend beyond the life of the 397 patent. 398

candidates.statement: Determining whether forfeiture has occurred requires analyzing if and when the events described 570 under the failure to market provision occurred. As seen in the statutory provision outlined 571 immediately above, application of this forfeiture provision requires a series of analyses based on 572 the timing of specific events. The statute directs that a forfeiture event occurs when the first 573 applicant fails to market the drug by the later of two dates. One of these dates is calculated under 574 item (aa) by determining the earlier of a date that is either 75 days after the first applicant’s 575 ANDA is approved (subitem (AA)) or 30 months after the date of submission of the first 576 applicant’s ANDA (subitem (BB)). The date determined under item (aa) then is compared to the 577 date as determined under item (bb). Item (bb) states that the occurrence of at least one of the 578 enumerated events with respect to a first applicant or any other applicant (which other applicant 579 has received tentative approval) as to each of the qualifying patents will begin a 75-day period 580 leading to possible forfeiture of exclusivity. These events include, very generally, when a court 581 enters a final decision that the patent is invalid or not infringed, a court signs a settlement order 582 or consent decree entering final judgment that includes a finding that the patent is invalid or not 583 infringed, or the patent information for the listed drug is withdrawn by the NDA holder. 52 For an 584 event to occur under item (bb) by any other applicant, the same other applicant must receive both 585
candidates.context: 51 Section 505(j)(5)(D)(i)(I) of the FD&C Act. tentative approval and a final court decision described in subitem (AA) or (BB). Forfeiture 586 under section 505(j)(5)(D)(i)(I) of the FD&C Act occurs if the first applicant fails to market by 587 the later of the dates under item (aa) or (bb). 588

candidates.statement: No. The FD&C Act provides that “[t]he 180-day exclusivity period […] shall be forfeited by a 975 first applicant if a forfeiture event occurs with respect to that first applicant.” 78 Neither this 976 statutory provision, nor any other, states that in forfeiting exclusivity, a first applicant becomes a 977 subsequent applicant whose ANDA can be approved only after the 180-day exclusivity period 978 has run. Thus, FDA interprets the statute such that a first applicant that has forfeited exclusivity 979 remains a first applicant and need not await expiration of 180-day exclusivity to obtain approval 980 of its ANDA. A first applicant that has forfeited exclusivity is subject to the same timetable for 981 approval that governs the approval of ANDAs for first applicants that remain eligible for 180- 982 day exclusivity. 79 Section 505(j)(5)(B)(iv) of the FD&C Act, which governs the running of 180- 983 day exclusivity, does not distinguish between first applicants that have forfeited eligibility for 984 180-day exclusivity and those that have not, providing instead only that a subsequent applicant’s 985 ANDA may be approved 180 days after the date of first commercial marketing by any first 986 applicant. In addition, once FDA has approved one or more ANDAs, commercial marketing by 987 any first applicant will trigger the 180-day exclusivity period for all the first applicant ANDAs, 988 even if the triggering applicant is the first applicant that forfeited its eligibility for exclusivity. 989
candidates.context: Q42. Does a first applicant that forfeited its eligibility for exclusivity become a 971 “subsequent applicant” blocked from final approval by other first applicants’ eligibility for 972 exclusivity? 973 For example, assume ANDA A and ANDA B are first applicants. ANDA A forfeits its 991 eligibility for 180-day exclusivity for failure to obtain tentative approval within 30 months but 992 ANDA B maintains its eligibility. ANDA A is not blocked from approval by ANDA B’s 180- 993 day exclusivity because ANDA A remains a first applicant. ANDA A also can trigger ANDA 994 B’s 180-day exclusivity. However, ANDA A will not itself block subsequent applicants from 995 approval. Only ANDA B, which retained eligibility for exclusivity, will block subsequent 996 applicants from approval. 997
